teaser: Two swans have vanished into one circle, split down the middle like a day and its night.
review_notes:
Size about 150 x 150 cm, oil on canvas: check.
Biographical situation in 1915 (age 52, living in Stockholm caring for her blind mother, pause of 1908-1912 after Rudolf Steiner's visit, temple cycle of 193 works completed in 1915): check details.
Swan series: 24 paintings, 1914-15, beginning with a black and a white swan: check count.
The tiny mark at the exact center looks like a small triangle in the reproduction; the interpretation is hedged.
Pink as the color of love in her notes, and the swan as an alchemical sign for the union of opposites: check.
Notebooks: over a hundred, about 26,000 pages: check.
Her sketch of a round temple with a spiral ramp: check.

lesson.text: In 1915 Hilma af Klint was 52 and nobody was waiting for her paintings. Europe was at war, though Sweden stayed out of it. She lived in Stockholm with her mother, who had gone blind and needed daily care. The modest income she had once made from portraits and landscapes mattered less to her each year.

What mattered was a secret project. Since 1906 she had been painting a vast cycle for an imaginary temple, guided, she believed, by spirits. She had broken off for four years, discouraged and busy nursing her mother. In 1912 she picked up the brush again. By 1915 the end was close.

“The Swan” is one of the last chapters: a series of 24 canvases. The first shows what the title promises, a white swan and a black swan meeting beak to beak across a dividing line. Then, picture by picture, the birds dissolve into geometry. By number 17 this is what remains.
Only two pieces of drawing hold this picture together.

lines.label: The seam
lines.text: A dead straight vertical cuts the disc in two. In the first swan paintings this was the line where the two birds met.

lines.label: The whole
lines.text: One circle contains both halves. They disagree about everything inside it, yet they share a single outline and a single center.

lesson.text: On the left, a white ring around a black disc: the two swans' colors, light and darkness with no shades between. On the right, the same space is divided differently, into blue, yellow and a pink core. Af Klint used blue for the feminine and yellow for the masculine. Pink, in her notes, is the color of love.
The series starts with two opposite creatures and ends with shapes. The subject never changes: how two opposing forces can belong to one whole.
Af Klint kept more than a hundred notebooks, some 26,000 pages, in which she tried to work out what her own paintings meant. She often said she painted them first and understood them later.

A black swan and a white swan were a familiar pair: the same bird as its own opposite. Alchemists, the early experimenters who dreamed of turning lead into gold, used the swan as a sign for the joining of opposites, and she read that kind of literature closely. What is hers alone is the decision to let the birds go.

lesson.title: Where halves meet
lesson.text: The edges tell you how carefully this simple image was made.

spots.title: White against blue
spots.text: At the top of the seam the white ring stops and the blue one starts, with no blending. The rings are the same width, so the border looks cut with a knife.

spots.title: The very center
spots.text: A tiny dark mark sits exactly where the seam crosses the middle, at the edge of the pink. It is the pivot of the whole canvas, like the pin hole left by a compass.

spots.title: The red field
spots.text: The background is not flat. Brick red is brushed on in visible, cloudy strokes, lighter and darker in patches, so the hard-edged disc seems to float in something warm and alive.

lesson.text: That contrast is worth remembering: a living, hand-brushed ground and a shape as exact as a diagram. The canvas is about 1.5 m square (5 ft), so the disc is roughly the size of your upper body. You stand in front of it as you would in front of a mirror.
In 1915, the year of this painting, she finished the temple cycle: 193 works in nine years. No temple was ever built, though she sketched one, a round building with a spiral ramp.

Targets, discs and hard edges would become a common language of abstract painting some fifty years later. Af Klint got there alone, in a Stockholm apartment, between caring for her mother and writing in her notebooks. She never saw this picture hang in a public exhibition. Does it look to you like something that was meant to stay hidden?

quiz.question: What did the first paintings of the Swan series show?
options: A white swan and a black swan meeting
A circle on a red ground
A temple with a spiral ramp
quiz.explanation: The series begins with two birds and gradually turns them into geometry.

quiz.question: Which colors fill the left half of the disc?
quiz.explanation: The left half keeps the two swans' colors, white and black.

quiz.question: What was af Klint's daily situation in 1915?
options: She was teaching at an art academy
She was traveling through wartime Europe
She was caring for her blind mother in Stockholm
quiz.explanation: She lived with her mother, who had gone blind and needed daily care.

quiz.question: What is the constant subject of the Swan series?
options: How opposites belong to one whole
quiz.explanation: Birds or shapes, the theme is the union of opposing forces.

quiz.question: How is the red background painted?
quiz.explanation: The ground is hand-brushed and uneven, unlike the exact disc.

facts.text: Sweden fought in the First World War while af Klint painted this.
By No. 17, the swans of the series have dissolved into pure geometry.
facts.explanation: Only a divided circle on a red ground remains.

facts.text: Af Klint completed her temple cycle of 193 works in 1915.
facts.explanation: She had begun it in 1906 and finished nine years later.
